clinicalPearls: Follows blunt ocular trauma, often years earlier, so a careful history of contusion injury is essential in unilateral glaucoma.
Gonioscopy shows an irregularly widened ciliary body band, torn iris processes and a receded iris root, best appreciated by comparison with the fellow eye.

The tear is between the longitudinal and circular muscle fibres of the ciliary body; the outflow obstruction, however, is caused by associated trabecular damage and scarring rather than the recession itself.
Glaucoma risk rises when recession exceeds around 180 to 270 degrees of the angle circumference.
Onset of raised pressure may be immediate, but a substantial proportion present years to decades after the original injury, mandating lifelong follow-up.
The fellow, uninjured eye carries an increased lifetime risk of developing primary open-angle glaucoma and should also be monitored.
Laser trabeculoplasty tends to respond poorly because the meshwork is scarred; medical therapy and filtration surgery are the mainstays.
Associated contusion findings such as sphincter tears, iridodialysis, phacodonesis and commotio retinae support the mechanism.
reference.pathophysiology: A blunt, rapid antero-posterior compression of the globe produces an equatorial expansion that transmits shearing forces to the anterior chamber angle. The classic lesion is a cleft within the ciliary body created by separation of the longitudinal from the circular muscle fibres, seen clinically as angle recession. Although the recession itself does not directly obstruct outflow, the same injury damages the adjacent trabecular meshwork, and over subsequent months to years a Descemet-like endothelial membrane proliferates across the damaged angle, the meshwork scleroses and scars, and trabecular outflow facility declines. The resulting chronic rise in intraocular pressure drives a glaucomatous optic neuropathy. Late scarring explains the characteristic delay between trauma and the onset of glaucoma.
additionalDifferentials: traumatic hyphaema with acute pressure rise
ghost cell glaucoma following vitreous haemorrhage
steroid-induced glaucoma from treatment of the original injury
additionalInvestigations: gonioscopy of both eyes to identify and quantify angle recession
ultrasound biomicroscopy or anterior segment optical coherence tomography of the angle
intraocular pressure measurement and diurnal phasing
optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer
dilated fundus examination for coexisting contusion retinopathy or choroidal rupture
optic disc photography for baseline documentation
redFlags: markedly raised pressure with a history of significant blunt trauma
progressive optic neuropathy in a previously injured eye
recurrent spontaneous hyphaema suggesting neovascularisation or fragile vessels
coexisting retinal detachment or dialysis on fundus examination
reference.prognosis: Glaucoma may develop many years after injury, so lifelong monitoring is required; with timely pressure control the prognosis is reasonable, but the scarred meshwork responds poorly to laser and surgical control can be challenging.
pitfalls: Failing to take a trauma history in unilateral glaucoma and missing the diagnosis.
Not examining the fellow eye, which carries an elevated risk of open-angle glaucoma.
Relying on laser trabeculoplasty, which is typically ineffective in a scarred angle.
Discharging a patient after early normal pressures despite extensive recession, when glaucoma may appear decades later.
Overlooking coexisting posterior segment contusion injury that also threatens vision.
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course, Glaucoma
management: Topical intraocular-pressure-lowering therapy, favouring aqueous suppressants such as beta-blockers, alpha-agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors alongside prostaglandin analogues, since the scarred meshwork limits outflow-dependent drugs
Incisional glaucoma surgery such as trabeculectomy or a drainage tube when pressure is uncontrolled medically, as laser trabeculoplasty responds poorly to the scarred angle
Lifelong monitoring of intraocular pressure, optic nerve and visual fields, given onset may be delayed years to decades after injury
Gonioscopy to document the extent of recession, with greater angle involvement carrying higher glaucoma risk
Surveillance of the fellow, uninjured eye for its increased lifetime risk of primary open-angle glaucoma
Referral to a glaucoma specialist for challenging pressure control and assessment for coexisting contusion injury
